newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium vows telecom market will be open in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Belgium vows telecom market will be open in 1998.

text.p: The Belgian government on Friday vowed to prepare the country for the liberalisation of the European telecommunications market next year.

"We have the firm intention to be ready for the liberalised market on January 1, 1998," Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told a news conference after a cabinet meeting which was devoted entirely to telecommunications issues.
His remarks came just one day after the European Commission said it was gearing up to react quickly to complaints about countries that are not opening their telecoms markets.
The Commission said that Belgium -- with Greece, Portugal and Spain -- was one of the countries which were way behind in meeting the European Union's deadline for full liberalisation.
Dehaene's centre-left government today agreed on a broad package of measures to open the Belgian telephone market, lower prices, increase consumer services and boost Internet use.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Telecommunications Elio di Rupo said there would be no limit on the number of telephone operators in Belgium next year.
He also said the government was working on regulations governing interconnections between competing networks and standardised telephone numbers.
"There can be no discrimination in interconnection, prices must be fair and will be public," he said, adding that a draft royal decree on the issue would be ready before the summer.

Di Rupo also said that all future operators in Belgium would use the same standardised telephone numbers and zonal prefixes. He added that by the year 2000, customers would be able to keep their number if they moved within the same telephone zone.
"Whether it is a German operator, a British operator or Belgacom, clients will enjoy so-called 'portability' of their phone numbers," he said.
Belgacom is 49.9 percent owned by a consortium including U.S. Ameritech, Singapore Telecom and Tele Danmark and three Belgian investors, following its partial privatisation in December 1995.
Di Rupo said he expected telephone costs to drop quickly next year, as foreign players moved into Belgium.
But he also warned that all players -- including the new entrants -- would have to offer a minimal service to customers.
"Connection charges will have to be the same for all clients, whether they live in the city or in a remote house in the country," he said.
He also said that phone companies would no longer be allowed to cut off customers' lines if they fail to pay their invoices.
"As long as customers respect a repayment schedule, companies will not be allowed to cut incoming calls. Phones must also always be available for emergency numbers," he added.

Di Rupo also said that the government planned to invite telecoms operators to enter bids for a third GSM mobile telephone network in Belgium. A formal bidding procedure will be opened with a view to choosing a third operator within a year and have a third sercive operational within two years.
Besides the telephone market, the government also took a series of measures aimed at easing Belgians' access to the electronic information highway.
The government will legalise encryption technologies, and is preparing legislation to give electronic signatures force of law.

Dehaene said that schools, libraries and hospitals would be able to get high-performance ISDN telephone lines at cut-rate prices, including a fixed number of free calls. Operators will be allowed to pass on the cost to the government.
"We want to stimulate young people's entry in the information society," Dehaene said.
